---
title: "Developing new functions in SITS"
format: html
---

## General principles

New functions that build on the `sits` API should follow the general principles below.

- The target audience for `sits` is the community of remote sensing experts with Earth Sciences background who want to use state-of-the-art data analysis methods with minimal investment in programming skills. The design of the `sits` API considers the typical workflow for land classification using satellite image time series and thus provides a clear and direct set of functions, which are easy to learn and master.

- For this reason, we welcome contributors that provide useful additions to the existing API, such as new ML/DL classification algorithms. In case of a new API function, before making a pull request please raise an issue stating your rationale for a new function.

- Most functions in `sits` use the S3 programming model with a strong emphasis on generic methods wich are specialized depending on the input data type. See for example the implementation of the `sits_bands()` function.

- Please do not include contributed code using the S4 programming model. Doing so would break the structure and the logic of existing code. Convert your code from S4 to S3.

- Use generic functions as much as possible, as they improve modularity and maintenance. If your code has decision points using `if-else` clauses, such as `if A, do X; else do Y` consider using generic functions.

- Functions that use the `torch` package use the R6 model to be compatible with that package. To convert `pyTorch` code to R and include it is straightforward. See for example, the code in `sits_tempcnn.R` and `api_torch.R`. 

- The sits code relies on the packages of the `tidyverse` to work with tables and list. We use `dplyr` and `tidyr` for data selection and wrangling, `purrr` and `slider` for loops on lists and table, `lubridate` to handle dates and times.

## Adherence to the `sits` data types

The `sits` package in built on top of three data types: time series tibble, data cubes and models. Most `sits` functions have one or more of these types as inputs and one of them as return values. The time series tibble contains data and metadata. The first six columns contain the metadata: spatial and temporal information, the label assigned to the sample, and the data cube from where the data has been extracted. The time_series column contains the time series data for each spatiotemporal location. All time series tibbles are objects of class `sits`.

The `cube` data type is designed to store metadata about image files. In principle, images which are part of a data cube share the same geographical region, have the same bands, and have been regularized to fit into a pre-defined temporal interval. Data cubes in `sits` are organized by tiles. A tile is an element of a satellite's mission reference system, for example MGRS for Sentinel-2 and WRS2 for Landsat. A `cube` is a tibble where each row contains information about data covering one tile. Each row of the cube tibble contains a column named `file_info`; this column contains a list that stores a tibble

The `cube` data type is specialised in `raster_cube` (ARD images), `vector_cube` (ARD cube with segmentation vectors). `probs_cube` (probabilities produced by classification algorithms on raster data), `probs_vector_cube`(probabilites generated by vector classification of segments),  `uncertainty_cube` (cubes with uncertainty information), and `class_cube` (labelled maps). See the code in `sits_plot.R` as an example of specialisation of `plot` to handle different classes of raster data.

All ML/DL models in `sits` which are the result of `sits_train` belong to the `ml_model` class. In addition, models are assigned a second class, which is unique to ML models (e.g, `rfor_model`, `svm_model`) and generic for all DL `torch` based models (`torch_model`). The class information is used for plotting models and for establishing if a model can run on GPUs.

## Literal values, error messages, and testing

The internal `sits` code has no literal values, which are all stored in the YAML configuration files `./inst/extdata/config.yml` and `./inst/extdata/config_internals.yml`. The first file contains configuration parameters that are relevant to users, related to visualisation and plotting; the second contains parameters that are relevant only for developers. These values are accessible using the `.conf` function. For example, the value of the default size for ploting COG files is accessed using the command `.conf["plot", "max_size"]`.

Error messages are also stored outside of the code in the YAML configuration file `./inst/extdata/config_messages.yml`. These values are accessible using the `.conf` function. For example, the error associated to an invalid NA value for an input parameter is accessible using th function `.conf("messages", ".check_na_parameter")`.

We strive for high code coverage (> 90\%). Every parameter of all `sits` function (including internal ones) is checked for consistency. Please see `api_check.R`.

## Using AI agents to develop new functions

AI coding agents, such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Posit Assistant, can help developers write new `sits` functions. These agents work directly on a local copy of the source code: they read files, search the code base, propose and edit code, and run tests in an R session. Used well, they reduce the effort needed to learn the internal structure of `sits`, which has more than 180 R source files and many internal APIs. Used without guidance, they tend to write generic R code that ignores the package conventions. For example, an agent might call `terra` functions directly, use `lapply()` loops, hard-code error messages, or access cube columns with `$`. Code written this way may work, but it is harder to maintain and will not be accepted as a contribution.

To avoid these problems, the `sits` repository includes a file called `AGENTS.md` in its root directory. `AGENTS.md` is an open convention for giving instructions to AI coding agents. It plays the same role for agents that `contributing.md` plays for human developers. Most agents read `AGENTS.md` automatically at the start of a session, so its rules guide every change the agent makes. Some agents look for their own file name instead. For this reason, the repository also contains a `CLAUDE.md` file that points Claude Code to `AGENTS.md`, so that all agents follow the same set of instructions. Both files are listed in `.Rbuildignore` and are not part of the package distributed on CRAN.

### What `AGENTS.md` contains

`AGENTS.md` is a short summary of the rules described in this chapter, written so that an agent can apply them. Its main sections are:

- *Repository map*: the layout of the package (`R/`, `src/`, `tests/`, `inst/extdata/`, `man/`), with notes on which files are generated automatically and must never be edited by hand, such as `NAMESPACE`, `man/*.Rd`, and `RcppExports.R`.

- *File organisation and naming*: exported functions go in `sits_<topic>.R` files and are named `sits_<name>()`. Internal code goes in `api_<topic>.R` files, and function names start with a dot and a domain prefix (`.raster_*`, `.cube_*`, `.tile_*`, `.bbox_*`). When adding a feature, the agent puts the user-facing entry point in a `sits_` file and the supporting code in the matching `api_` file.

- *Internal API usage*: agents must use the existing internal APIs instead of handling objects directly. All raster input and output goes through `api_raster.R`, never through direct calls to `terra::`. Cube and tile fields are read with accessors such as `.cube_bands()`, `.cube_timeline()`, `.tile_bbox()`, and `.tile_path()`. Loops over tiles use `.cube_foreach_tile()` or `slider`. Before writing new helper code, the agent should check whether an existing internal function already does the job.

- *Programming model*: new functions must be S3 generics, starting with `.check_set_caller()` followed by `UseMethod()`, with methods for each input class (`sits`, `raster_cube`, `tbl_df`, `default`). S4 is not allowed. R6 is used only for `torch` models, following `sits_tempcnn.R` and `api_torch.R`. This section also describes the core data types: time series tibbles, data cubes and their subclasses, and `ml_model` objects.

- *Code style*: four-space indentation, lines of about 80 characters, the `tidyverse`/`sf`/`terra` stack, and `purrr` and `slider` instead of the `apply` family.

- *No literal values*: configuration values come from `config.yml` and `config_internals.yml`, error messages from `config_messages.yml`, and colours from `config_colors.yml`. All of them are read with `.conf()`.

- *Parameter checking, documentation, and testing*: inputs are checked with the `.check_*` functions in `api_check.R`. Exported functions have full `roxygen2` documentation, with examples wrapped in `if (sits_run_examples())`, while internal functions use `@noRd`. Tests are written with `testthat`, one file per topic, focusing on the public functions.

- *Build and verification*: the agent should run `devtools::document()`, the relevant tests, and `devtools::check()` before it reports that the work is done. Because the full test suite can take hours, the agent should run only the tests for the function it changed, for example with `devtools::test(filter = "bands")`.

- *Commits*: the agent must never commit on the user's behalf. The developer reviews all changes and commits them.

### A suggested workflow

The following workflow works well when using an AI agent to develop a new `sits` function.

1. Clone the `sits` repository and start the agent in its root directory, so that `AGENTS.md` is read automatically. If you use an agent that does not read `AGENTS.md`, tell it explicitly to read the file before starting.

2. Describe the new function precisely. Give its name and purpose, the input data types it should accept, its parameters and their defaults, and the expected output. Point to an existing function with a similar structure. For example:

    > *Write a new generic function `sits_band_stats()` that computes, for each band, the median and the interquartile range of the values of a time series tibble. Follow the pattern of `sits_bands.R`, with methods for `sits` and `default`. Put the helper code in an `api_` file, add the error messages to `config_messages.yml`, write roxygen documentation with an example, and add a test file. Run only the new tests.*

3. Ask the agent to explore the code first and present a plan before it edits any files. Check that the plan reuses existing internal functions (`.cube_*`, `.tile_*`, `.raster_*`, `.check_*`) rather than creating new ones that duplicate them.

4. Review the proposed code against the rules in `AGENTS.md` and in this chapter. Look for direct calls to `terra::`, use of `$` on cubes or tiles, `if-else` decisions on object class instead of S3 methods, literal values or messages in the code, and missing parameter checks.

5. Run the new tests and `devtools::check()`, and make sure the package stays free of CRAN check notes, warnings, and errors.

6. Review the full set of changes yourself before committing them and opening a pull request. As for any other contribution, open an issue explaining why a new API function is needed before submitting it.

AI agents speed up development, but they do not replace the developer's judgement. Agents can produce code that looks plausible but is wrong, especially for scientific algorithms, where results must be checked against known reference values. The author of a pull request is responsible for all the code it contains, whether it was written by hand or with the help of an agent. Contributors who find that the agent repeatedly makes the same kind of mistake are encouraged to suggest an improvement to `AGENTS.md`, so that future contributors benefit from the clarified rule.
